title: Topological Data Analysis of NFL Defensive Formations: Does Persistent Homology Predict Coverage Breakdowns Beyond Standard Geometric Baselines?
content: The availability of high-resolution optical tracking data in the National Football League (NFL) has enabled the analysis of player position on a frame-by-frame basis. However, most prior work, including continuous-time play valuation [25], offensive player valuation [26], completion probability [10], route classification [8], and pass coverage identification [11], has focused on local, pairwise, or clustering-based statistics rather than global geometric properties of the formation. This paper investigates the predictive value of topological features, extracted using persistent homology [6,12], over common geometric baselines for real-time defensive formations in the NFL, using coverage breakdowns as the outcome of interest. Using the NFL Big Data Bowl 2021 public dataset [19], we reconstructed 2D point clouds of the positions of the defenders in the 0.6 seconds preceding a pass release. We extracted topological features using the Vietoris–Rips filtration and evaluated their predictive value using logistic regression and cross-validated AUC scores. We compared topological features against three common geometric baselines: defender convex hull area, mean nearest-defender distance, and mean defender spread. We also performed a blind confirmatory analysis on a disjoint subset of data to evaluate generalizability. Topological features showed significant association with coverage breakdowns (p < 0.01, 1,360 plays across all 17 weeks of the 2018 regular season). However, this association did not yield predictive benefit over simple geometric summaries (Baseline AUC: 0.6811, 95% CI [0.677, 0.686]; Combined AUC: 0.6742, 95% CI [0.667, 0.682]). This was true even for the subset of plays for which the baseline model was least certain. A redundancy analysis suggested that geometric features explained only 3 to 9 percent of the variance of the topological features, supporting the idea that the two sets of features are not strongly redundant. Even so, whatever information is in the topological features that is not captured by geometry does not appear to be predictive. We suspect that the reason for this lies in the sparsity of the point cloud (7 to 8 points): the topological features captured only a single, coarse property of the formation, the size of the largest gap. For a point cloud this sparse, persistent homology does not appear to provide much benefit over simpler geometric summaries, and we consider this a useful boundary condition for the application of topological data analysis more generally, in line with calls to report null and boundary findings in the scientific literature [16].
